title: Our cultural values
content:
## The values

1.   **[Ambitious, long-term impact](https://80000hours.org/2026/11/our-cultural-values/#ambitious-long-term-impact)**  
 Increase wellbeing for moral patients over the long term.
2.   **[Team mentality](https://80000hours.org/2026/11/our-cultural-values/#team-mentality)**  
 We’re teammates with each other, our users, and the community.
3.   **[Prioritisation and urgency](https://80000hours.org/2026/11/our-cultural-values/#prioritisation-and-urgency)**  
 Make the most important things happen soon.
4.   **[Good judgement](https://80000hours.org/2026/11/our-cultural-values/#good-judgement)**  
 Reason well and show your work, then make the call and keep updating.
5.   **[Proactive ownership](https://80000hours.org/2026/11/our-cultural-values/#proactive-ownership)**  
 Take responsibility and be generative.

Ambitious, long-term impact is our anchoring value that the others act in service of. If there’s a conflict, we prioritise it first (though not by violating side constraints or [naively maximising](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/toby-ord-perils-of-maximising-good/)).

## How we use them

Our values are the high-level principles we use when making day-to-day decisions at 80,000 Hours. They guide our plans, actions, and hiring to help us pursue our [strategic focus](https://80000hours.org/2026/05/our-strategy-at-80000-hours/) by:

*   Keeping salient what’s important
*   Providing rules of thumb for how to act under uncertainty
*   Shaping our team and practices
*   Keeping everyone on the same page as we grow

The values are partly descriptive — capturing what’s already important and distinctive about 80,000 Hours’ culture — and partly aspirational — motivating how we’d like to act going forward.

## In more detail

### 1. Ambitious, long-term impact

**Increase wellbeing for moral patients over the long term**

The purpose of everything we do is to maximise our long-term positive impact.[1](https://80000hours.org/2026/11/our-cultural-values/#fn-1) It underlies our decision making, strategic focus, and orientation to our work. We’re here to help others, including those who don’t have a voice today (like future generations and digital beings) and we want to be ambitious in how we go about it.

We think that if 80,000 Hours fulfils its potential, we’ll have made a major contribution to some of the world’s most pressing problems — by being a main source of dedicated talent for these problems and by improving the world’s position going into the arrival of AGI. These are hard goals, but with ambition and focus we think we can make a dent.

More concretely, we aim to:

*   **Keep in mind our high-level goals when making decisions.** We want to orient to our work with compassion for our beneficiaries; favour actions that pay off over the long term, rather than too narrowly prioritising short-term outcomes and metrics; and ask ourselves whether our actions will move the needle on our strategic goals.
*   **Regularly ask ourselves how our work can have a lot more impact.** We think the best version of a project can matter far more than a good one, so it’s worth spending some time checking whether there are things we should be deprioritising or ways to reorient to a project to make it much more ambitious.
*   **Avoid anchoring too hard on what’s safely achievable.** We want to take high expected value bets, even if this means sometimes failing. It’s valuable to be generative and innovative, and we’ll aim to celebrate when we take sensible risks that don’t pay off.
*   **Build capacity, including our own,** so that we can achieve more in the future. This should happen both at the team-growth level and in terms of cultivating personal development and energy.

### 2. Team mentality

**We’re teammates with each other, our users, and the community**

Our goal of increasing wellbeing over the long term is demanding, but we’re not working on the project alone: 80,000 Hours is an org made up of incredibly motivated, caring individuals; we have many users (and potential users) who are excited to use their careers to do the most good; and we’re working within the EA and AIS communities, which have many shared values and goals with us.

By cultivating this feeling we’re on the same team, we’ll naturally orient to one another with lots of the values here. By applying the following examples of cooperation, trust, and mutual caring both internally and externally, we can better achieve our goals since they’ll help us stay coordinated and motivated longer term.

More concretely:

#### Cooperation and trust

*   **Use the red-face test** to check whether our actions are honest and credible: ask ourselves whether it’d feel embarrassing to describe our plan to someone whose integrity we deeply respect, and if so, reconsider.
*   **Treat people like adults,** saying what we actually believe in a way that helps them to make a good decision by their own lights.
    *   We want to be persuasive but not manipulative, which includes: communicating transparently; using strong reasoning; not using cherrypicked facts or saying things that will predictably mislead users; avoiding too much clickbait or hyperbole; not using negative emotions like fear, anxiety, or inadequacy as a persuasion tactic; etc.
    *   We also want to communicate clearly and kindly in cases where we can’t help someone (which will come up often, as people have varied needs and skills and we have to prioritise). Give an honest picture and point them elsewhere if relevant.

*   **Say what’s true and necessary, with kindness.** By sharing ideas, thoughts, and feedback constructively, we can progress conversations efficiently and help others improve.
*   **Disagree productively.** We aim to assume good faith and be curious, voice disagreements directly and early, be proactive about resolving frictions, and get behind a decision once it’s been made.
*   **Give visibility by default.** By working in public when it’s not too costly, we can increase our surface area for solving problems, learn faster, and avoid duplication of effort. This applies to:
    *   Making information, decisions, and thought processes visible in Slack, so others can contribute ideas and feedback. Most of our Slack channels are shared org-wide for this purpose.
    *   Sharing learnings and [what we’re up to](https://80000hours.org/about/credibility/reviews/) with other organisations when we can.
    *   Giving users an accurate representation of our views, so they can make informed decisions.

*   **Value others’ time.** We want to present information in an intuitive, user-friendly way which prioritises clarity. This includes giving orienting notes and only asking for what we need.

#### Mutual caring

*   **Show appreciation** for colleagues, other organisations, users, and people who want to contribute but aren’t in a position to help right now.
*   **Help others achieve their goals** by giving feedback, lending our skills, holding each other accountable, and noticing when someone is hitting their limits.
    *   We give [Watch Team Back Up](https://thewholesky.wordpress.com/2021/09/27/watch-team-backup/) (WTBU) — flagging potential mistakes or balls that might be dropped, without assuming that the person wouldn’t have caught it.

### 3. Prioritisation and urgency

**Make the most important things happen soon**

Some plausible [AI timelines](https://80000hours.org/ai/guide/when-will-agi-arrive/) mean that we might not have long before the world looks very different, so we want to make the most important work happen soon. To achieve that, we need to focus on the things we judge to be the most valuable and deprioritise everything else. And we need to approach our priorities with appropriate urgency — working hard and efficiently, but not unsustainably.

More concretely:

#### Prioritisation

*   **Act on what’s most important.** There are many promising opportunities, but we think that the most effective usually have far more impact than the median, and we still face steep tradeoffs for capacity. To get the most valuable stuff done, we need to be in triage mode.
    *   Although we can’t always be confident in what’s most important, we can make a reasonable guess by comparing projects, using the [scale-neglectedness-solveability framework](https://80000hours.org/articles/problem-framework/), and getting input from others.
    *   And we should try to avoid things that look good just because they’re recent, shiny, or socially desirable.

*   **Say no to everything else.** To focus on the top priorities, we need to be ruthless about turning everything else down… even though that’s often painful. We should celebrate saying no, and remember that doing so enables us to ship the most useful deliverables sooner.
    *   This also means evaluating whether there’s anything that we’re currently doing that we should drop — seeking to avoid the sunk cost fallacy, practising the reversal test,[2](https://80000hours.org/2026/11/our-cultural-values/#fn-2) and periodically clearing out accumulated low-value tasks.

#### Urgency

*   **Be efficient.** We think about what the best route is to the outcome we want, act decisively, and prioritise getting unblocked if something is slowing us down.
    *   Being efficient often means moving quickly through actions, but it sometimes means slowing down to avoid hard-to-fix or time-intensive mistakes. Slowing down and double checking particularly makes sense in places where we’re interacting with a large number of users, handling sensitive data, or making an irreversible call.

*   **Value time highly,** both that of ourselves and others. We take sensible opportunities to trade money with time, say no to things that don’t meet our bar, and look for ways to improve our output.
*   **Point out ways to minimise bureaucracy.** We want our systems to be useful and clear, and appreciate opportunities to streamline things. We use RAPIDs to make major decisions, minimising whose agreement is required while creating opportunities for input to increase transparency and improve the quality of decisions.
*   **Don’t confuse urgency with working more hours.** We want people to use their work time wisely, not work more than is sustainable for them. We need to jog so that we can sprint when we need to.
    *   That’s not to say it isn’t valuable when people work a lot (it is!), but it only pays off if it’s sustainable.

### 4. Good judgement

**Reason well and show your work, then make the call and keep updating.**

80,000 Hours tries to answer very challenging questions — about the world, our advice, and our strategy — under a lot of uncertainty. We can’t wait for certainty before acting, so we act on our current best guess while continuing to look out for and correct mistakes, letting us move fast while staying grounded.

More concretely, we aim to:

*   **Take a [scout mindset](https://forum.effectivealtruism.org/topics/scout-mindset):** we’re aiming to find out what’s true rather than be right, which means holding our views as a best guess and updating when the world tells us something new.
    *   We want to stay curious, weigh the evidence by its strength, be wary of motivated reasoning and confirmation bias, and avoid getting attached to our beliefs.
    *   To facilitate this, we regularly seek advice and feedback from external experts, in addition to others on the team, and aim to show that it’s okay to change our minds.

*   **Show our work,** sharing the reasoning behind our conclusions and how confident we are, rather than just giving the bottom line. This allows others to weigh in, build on our thinking, and catch mistakes.
    *   We also do this in our external content so users can make an informed decision — we aim to be appropriately hedged in our views, back up key claims, and correct things we no longer endorse. We balance this with being engaging and forceful.

*   **Be decisive.** We don’t feel like we need certainty before making a decision. Instead, we aim to form a sensible, resilient view, act on it, and update our views as we get more information.
*   **Periodically ask, “How might this be wrong?”** The world is fast-moving and complex, and we’re fallible, so it’s important to keep looking for mistakes and evidence that will improve our actions.
    *   For important decisions and projects, we often run a pre-mortem and write out uncertainties, alternatives, and counter-arguments.
    *   There are lots of topics we’ve changed our minds on in the past, and we expect there to be many more in the future!

*   **Notice our confusion** and ask probing questions to help detangle it.

### 5. Proactive ownership

**Take responsibility and be generative**

Whatever your role, doing it well adds to what 80,000 Hours can achieve overall — whether that’s advisors owning the quality of their advice, hosts feeling responsible for every episode they ship, or ops staff delivering their remits consistently well. We want everyone to fully own their remits and hold each other to a high standard in doing this. Ownership means looking after an area or problem from end to end, taking responsibility for how it goes overall, thinking expansively about it, and deciding how much to invest.

More concretely, we aim to:

*   **Take responsibility** for our remits going well, rather than deferring to how things have been done before or relying on managers to check in.
    *   Act as the owner of the responsibility, rather than the operator of a task: it’s up to each individual to prioritise appropriately, look after end-to-end delivery, seek out improvements, and post-mortem when things go wrong.

*   **Show our manager that we’re owning it.** Giving our manager confidence that we’re fully handling a responsibility and will seek their help if we need it means that they can take a step back from thinking about it.
    *   This looks like giving managers visibility, showing our reasoning, not dropping balls without communicating first, and owning mistakes. We strive to ask for help when we need it and escalate potential problems early, and to notice places where we think we could take on more ownership and sync up with our manager about these.

*   **Decide what not to prioritise.** Owning something well also means deciding when it doesn’t make sense to invest, and it’ll sometimes be the right call to just maintain business as usual. We aim to make that call deliberately.
*   **Notice gaps and ownership ambiguities,** flagging balls that are potentially being dropped, AORs that don’t exist, or problems that no one feels responsible for.
*   **Be thoughtful about our responsibilities** — thinking about what we’re trying to achieve overall, how things might go wrong, how to communicate about them, and what we’ll need to do to keep them running well.
*   **Be generative** in the areas we’re prioritising, going beyond day-to-day running to become an expert in our area.
    *   If this is going well, we should be having lots of ideas for how to automate, improve, and expand the responsibility, and be seeking out more ideas from others.
    *   And we should be using AI to figure out how to make things work better and more efficiently.

*   **Grow into our remits.** Be reflective about how we can improve, regularly gather feedback, and invest time in developing the skills to fully own our current (and future!) responsibilities.

title: The emotions of voting
content:
**Futility:** It might feel like it doesn’t matter.  
**Fear:** Of choosing wrong, or doing it wrong.  
**Responsibility:** It isn’t given, it’s taken. Which is why so many leave it on the table.  
**Possibility:** Showing up to have your say could change things for the better.  
**Identity:** This is what people like us do, it’s part of being in this community.  
**Defiance:** Some would rather you stay home. Your vote is a limit on their plans.  
**Gratitude:** For the people who came before, and for the ones who never had the chance.  
**Dignity:** Because for a moment, everyone ought to have the same impact.  
**Solidarity:** Standing with the others when they choose to stand with us.  
**Hope:** This may be our best chance to make things better.

That’s a lot to dance with from one single action. I think it’s worth it.

title: Tourist Posts a Photo to a Facebook Group, Accidentally Discovering 120-Million-Year-Old Dinosaur Footprint
content:
“So, how was your vacation?”

“Good, thanks. Ate some great food. Saw the sights. Really managed to unwind. Oh, and I discovered a 120-million-year-old dinosaur footprint.”

That’s the story 32-year-old Pichai Prathetsena can tell after returning from Phu Phra Bat National Park in Thailand. Having happened upon the deep indentation on his travels, Prathetsena uploaded a photo of the footprint to Facebook, where it was spotted by the government.

The original photo from Pichai Prathetsena, posted to a Facebook page called “What Is This Creature?” _Credit: Pichai Prathetsena_

Experts were soon on the scene to identify the 11.4-inch-by-10.2-inch print, and the park was closed so the area could be properly examined. The three-toed footprint turned out to be one of six, all of which date back to the Early Cretaceous.

These are trace fossils, which means they’re not actual remains but rather indirect evidence of an ancient animal—in this case, deep impressions in soft ground that later hardens, preserving the footprints like a cast.

The size and depth of the impressions, as well as the distance between them, give archaeologists some clues to the dinosaur’s weight, dimensions, stride length, and gait. To that end, it’s estimated that this particular dino, a carnivorous theropod, walked on hind legs that measured around 4 feet, 8 inches, with an estimated length of more than 20 feet. That puts it in the same category as the one-ton _Siamotyrannus isanensis_, previously discovered in Thailand, but more research is necessary to fully identify the species.

It’s estimated that the print comes from a dino around 20 feet long. _Credit: Thailand Department of Mineral Resources_

Government agencies are now working to preserve the footprints and reduce further erosion and water damage. In fact, according to the Thai Department of Mineral Resources on [Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/DMRTH/posts/pfbid0ZAQdQMexvG2D1ZPeoMdFq6ueKpfNnCmbpSdPikx1LBUcdF5HWRNPg7q2JmcsA6WSl), the site could be developed into a geological and fossil research hub.

Dinosaur footprints have been discovered in Thailand for decades—a total of 25 dinosaur species have been uncovered there to date, including 13 that haven’t been located anywhere else—but these are the first prints of a carnivorous dinosaur to be found in the Udon Thani Province. Many of the finds have also been linked to citizen scientists.

Experts on site in the Phu Phra Bat National Park. _Credit: Thailand Department of Mineral Resources_

So it’s a good reminder to keep your eyes open and your phone camera close while you’re on vacation. After all, you never know what you [might stumble across](https://nautil.us/this-giant-waterlily-species-was-discovered-via-instagram-1285947). ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: The Monstrous Raptors That Threatened Our Ancestors
content:
Our ancestors may not have lived among traditional dinosaurs, but they did live among avian dinosaurs. Massive birds of prey with monstrous wingspans darkened the skies for the bulk of hominin evolution, and it’s possible they shaped our development, according to a new [report](https://www.bbc.com/future/article/20261028-predatory-birds-the-size-of-a-small-aircraft-once-flocked-the-skies-some-of-them-ate-humans) by the BBC.

Before Lucy, one of the earliest hominin relatives discovered was unearthed from a Limestone quarry in Taung, South Africa, in 1924 alongside a cache of animal bones. The 2.8-million-year-old skull, belonging to a toddler, was termed the Taung child and a member of the newly named species _Australopithecus africanus_. Seventy years later, paleontologists analyzing the bones found alongside the Taung skull [suggested](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1995JHumE..29..275B/abstract) they bore an eerie resemblance to the kind of skeletal assemblage you might find in the nest of a large bird of prey.

**Read more: “[New Feathered Dinosaur is the First Megaraptor Discovered in Europe](https://nautil.us/new-feathered-dinosaur-is-the-first-megaraptor-discovered-in-europe-1285813)”**

Following up on that study in 2006, Scott McGraw and a team of fellow anthropologists compared markings on the Taung child’s skull to those on the skulls of monkeys that were snatched up by the African crowned eagle. According to their [analysis](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/epdf/10.1002/ajpa.20420), the markings matched. Distinctive talon scratches along the eye sockets of both primates told a gruesome story of the Taung child’s death.

This constant fear of death from above may have altered the course of human evolution, per McGraw and archaeologist James Cole of Brighton University. The threat of birds of prey cannonballing out of the skies to snatch a child may have fueled the need for sociality, forcing hominin ancestors to band together to warn one another. Among other primate species, the alarm calls for terrestrial threats like lions and leopards are the same, while eagles get their own distinctive sound. McGraw, Cole, and others say this kind of vocal signalling flexibility could represent the [roots of language](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/epdf/10.1002/evan.21378).

While any imprint these flying leviathans left on human evolution is largely speculative, the cultural impact they had is closer to undeniable. Teratorns, massive condor-like predators that soared above the Americas until as recently as 10,000 years ago, may have been the inspiration for the mythical Thunderbird of Native American folklore. Additionally, New Zealand’s Haast’s eagle, with an eight-foot wingspan, could have been the source of Maori legends of Te Hokioi, a child-grabbing raptor with talons like panther’s paws.

For better or worse, both species are now gone forever. The bird with the largest wingspan (12 feet, a far cry from teratorn species’ 20-feet) is an albatross, only feared by fish. It’s a loss to the natural world, but at least we don’t have to check the daily raptor report before sending our kids to school. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Bizarre Fruit-Eating “Hell Chicken” Suggests Dinosaurs Played a Role in Flowering Plant Evolution
content:
In the late Cretaceous, fruit was a brand new innovation. Flowering plants first evolved during this period and started taking over on land, replacing cone-bearing plants. But who was eating this newly evolved produce?

While the armored ankylosaurs and duck-billed hadrosaurs may have incorporated fruit into their diets, they still mostly subsisted on leafy plants. Now, paleontologists have unearthed a dinosaur that appears to be a specialized fruit-feeder, describing it for the first time in a study [published](http://dx.doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-78343-w) in _Nature Communications_.

**Read more: “**[**The Strawberry Is a Frankenfruit**](https://nautil.us/the-strawberry-is-a-frankenfruit-1263209)**”**

The species was discovered in the famed Hell Creek Formation, a sprawling fossil-rich region covering Montana, North Dakota, and South Dakota. Its final resting place gave the species its genus name, _Infernogallus_, or “hell chicken.” Roughly the size of a turkey, this hell chicken was an odd duck.

“It’s pretty rare for animals to become specialized for a diet of fruit, so when it happens, it comes with some remarkable adaptations,” study author Thomas Dudgeon of the University of Toronto said in a [statement](https://www.rom.on.ca/news-releases/rare-fossil-discovery-reveals-new-dinosaur-species-were-specialized-fruit-eaters). “The anatomy of _Infernogallus_ is bizarre among dinosaurs, and we quickly realized that we were dealing with something special.”

The species belonged to the caenagnathid group, a family of toothless feathered oviraptors, but CT scans of its skull indicate it preferred fruit to eggs. According to the researchers, its musculature gave the small dino chewing mechanics that were adept at mashing up pulpy fiber. Its palatal bones (forming the roof of its mouth) arched downward, meaning certain muscles faced front-to-back and not up and down. This allowed the dinosaur to slide its beak back and forth in a chewing motion, rather than a vertical chomp.

The team says this jaw architecture is fairly rare in the animal kingdom, but present in omnivorous mammals (like humans) as well as the vulturine parrot, which eats fruit. It could also mean dinosaurs played a larger role in the evolution of fruit-bearing plants than previously thought, helping the immobile flora disperse its seeds.

“The strange skull of _Infernogallus_ is an exciting find because it reveals surprising insights into dinosaur evolution and feeding specialization,” study author David Evans of the University of Toronto explained. “This discovery shows that we still have a lot to learn about the world of T. rex, and about dinosaurs more generally.” ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: A Collapsing Star Produced an Afterglow Brighter Than Its Galaxy
content:
Much of what we understand about the universe comes from interpreting the light patterns that hit our telescopes—from the smallest twinkles [of distant stars](https://nautil.us/this-supernova-death-of-a-star-broke-all-the-rules-1283530) to giant clouds of dust and gas. That’s what makes the recent find from NASA’s Fermi Gamma Ray Space Telescope, which sits in low Earth orbit, so exciting: it’s one of the brightest bursts of light in decades.

The flash is an intense afterglow following a gamma-ray burst (GRB). While the gamma-ray light was modest, the afterglow was incredibly bright—among the brightest 1 percent of observed events compared in a newly published [study](https://doi.org/10.3847/2041-8213/aea990).

**Read more: “[Dead Star Offers a Glimpse Into Our Solar System’s Future](https://nautil.us/dead-star-offers-a-glimpse-into-our-solar-systems-future-1286164)”**

Why was the afterglow so much brighter than the event itself?

The team behind the study thinks it has to do with the angle of our view. “We see hundreds of GRBs every year, but the oddballs are the most informative ones,” study author Roberto Ricci said in a [statement](https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/1149470). “We could explain individual features of this burst, but fitting them all into the same picture proved much harder.”

What happened first was the death of a massive star around 2 billion light-years away. As stars collapse, they shoot out brief, intense jets of gamma rays from their poles, which was the first flash spotted by the Fermi telescope on March 10th.

As the jets of gamma rays continue to spread out through space, they collide with the surrounding gas and start accelerating particles, which glow with energy released as radiation (i.e., the afterglow). The GRB 260310A afterglow brightened gradually over several hours, until it was outshining its galaxy. It then faded, only to brighten again weeks afterward in the X-ray spectrum. That may have been the light from the narrow core of the gamma-ray burst finally escaping, the astronomers say.

Such an intense, long-lasting afterglow suggests that what would have been dismissed as a fairly standard gamma-ray burst may in fact have been much more intense, viewed from the right angle. “What appeared to us as an unremarkable GRB might have looked like a monster explosion to an observer looking straight down the jet’s core,” study author Yu-Han Yang said in a [statement](https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/1149470). “Our models suggest that the explosion packed roughly a billion years of the sun’s energy output into a pencil-thin beam.”

With increased telescope performance and broader sky-mapping capabilities, scientists hope to capture more gamma-ray bursts from a greater range of angles in the future—which will, in turn, improve our understanding of how giant stars die off.

After all, there’s a lot that you can glean from a beam of light.

title: Listen to the Earliest Known Recordings of a Nearly Dead American Language
content:
A University of Cambridge linguist has uncovered a treasure trove containing the earliest known recordings of Creole language and analyzed them for the first time in a study [published](http://dx.doi.org/10.25894/ldd.3083) in _Language Documentation & Description_. The recordings were taken by famed Black linguist Lorenzo Dow Turner, who studied Gullah languages spoken by Black Americans living in South Carolina and traveled to Sierra Leone in search of the dialect’s African influences.

In 1935, Turner hauled equipment weighing over 100 pounds down to New Orleans to capture the voices of Creole speakers living there. He turned to a network of Black doctors to facilitate the sessions, using their waiting rooms as makeshift recording studios. “These were trusted spaces for the participants during the era of Jim Crow segregation, and, crucially, were wired for electricity,” study author Oliver Mayeux, who pieced together Turner’s trip from his notes, said in a [statement](https://www.cam.ac.uk/stories/louisiana-creole-earliest-spoken-audio).

Lorenzo Dow Turner. _Credit: Amistad Research Center, Tulane University_

Creole, a rich linguistic gumbo featuring a French base with Indigenous, Spanish, and English peppered in, is virtually extinct today. Turner never got to analyze the recordings himself (potentially because of funding issues), but now they’re offering insights into the dialect that written transcripts can’t provide.

[Audio 5](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/2026/11/Emma-Benoit-extract-2-1.wav)

An excerpt of Lorenzo Dow Turner’s interview with Mrs. Emma Benoit (1868-1939), a sharecropper who had 16 children (four adopted) and was a widow for 20 years. _Credit: Archives of Traditional Music at Indiana University Bloomington_

“Turner’s lost recordings contain far more linguistic diversity than the texts we relied upon until now,” Mayeux explained. “This is the language of the levees and cane fields. The language that drifted out from French Quarter saloons along with early jazz music at the turn of the last century.”

According to Mayeux, the language would have been indecipherable to classic French speakers at the time. It differs from its mother language in key respects, with no gender or number agreement and agglutinated nouns (articles and nouns smushed together, like _lapolis_ for “policemen”).

“Africans with little common language were forced onto plantations where French was the language of administration,” Mayeux explained. “Everybody is learning approximations of French and then approximations of approximations. Quite quickly, a new language is born.”

Beyond the technical aspects of the Creole language, the recordings also capture the colorful lives of the participants. One woman, Odelia Edmond, recounted her devilish youth spent hiding in church and snatching veils from brides, her run-ins with a local legend who sold voodoo accoutrement, and her first husband’s untimely demise.

[Audio 6](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/2026/11/Zozo-Labrique-Odelia-Edmond-extract-1.wav)

An excerpt of Lorenzo Dow Turner’s interview with Odélia Edmond (1862-1951). _Credit: Archives of Traditional Music at Indiana University Bloomington_

“Edmond is an extraordinary character,” Mayeux said. “I found a newspaper record from when she was arraigned for battery. She had a husband who was murdered, after which she remarried. In the recording she says, ‘I was so glad when they killed him’.”

It’s a compelling portrait of a culture and language that have all but disappeared from Louisiana. Fewer than 10,000 people speak the language today, although this research might give a boost to efforts to revive the dialect. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: I Feel, Therefore I Am: Neuroscientist Antonio Damasio the Consciousness of the Body
content:
[![Image 1: I Feel, Therefore I Am: Neuroscientist Antonio Damasio the Consciousness of the Body](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/feelingknowing_damasio.jpg?fit=320%2C468&ssl=1)](https://www.amazon.com/Feeling-Knowing-Making-Minds-Conscious/dp/1524747556/?tag=braipick-20)

“A purely disembodied emotion is a nonentity,” William James wrote in his revolutionary theory of [how our bodies affect our feelings](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/01/11/what-is-an-emotion-william-james/) just before [the birth of neuroscience](https://www.themarginalian.org/2017/02/23/beautiful-brain-santiago-ramon-y-cajal/) — a science still young, which has already revolutionized our understanding of the cosmos inside the cranium as much as the first century of telescopic astronomy [revolutionized](https://www.themarginalian.org/2019/01/02/perspective/) our understanding of our place in the universe.

Meanwhile, ninety miles inland from William James, while Walt Whitman was redoubling his metaphysical insistence that “the body includes and is the meaning, the main concern… and is the soul,” Emily Dickinson was writing in one of her [science-prescient poems](https://www.themarginalian.org/2020/08/06/patti-smith-reads-emily-dickinson/):

> The Brain — is wider than the Sky —  
>  For — put them side by side —  
>  The one the other will contain  
>  With ease — and you — beside —
> 
> 
> The Brain is deeper than the sea —  
>  For — hold them — Blue to Blue —  
>  The one the other will absorb —  
>  As sponges — Buckets — do —

[![Image 2](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/04/margaretcook_leavesofgrass16.jpg?resize=680%2C864&ssl=1)](https://society6.com/product/the-night-follows-along-with-millions-of-suns-and-sleep-and-restoring-darkness_print?sku=s6-8967977p4a1v45?curator=brainpicker)

Art by Margaret Cook from [a rare 1913 edition](https://www.themarginalian.org/2018/04/11/leaves-of-grass-margaret-cook/) of _Leaves of Grass_. (Available [as a print](https://society6.com/product/the-night-follows-along-with-millions-of-suns-and-sleep-and-restoring-darkness_print?sku=s6-8967977p4a1v45?curator=brainpicker))

It is the task, the destiny of science to concretize with evidence what the poets have always intuited and imagized in abstraction: that we are infinitely more miraculous and infinitely less important than we thought. The universe without, which made us and every star-dusted atom of our consciousness, is ever-vaster and more complex than we suppose it to be; the universe within, which makes the universe without and renders our entire experience of reality through the telescopic lens of our consciousness, is ever-denser and more complex than we suppose it to be.

A century and a half after James, neuroscientist [Antonio Damasio](https://www.themarginalian.org/tag/antonio-damasio/) picks up an empirical baton where Dickinson had left a torch of intuition. In his revelatory book **_[Feeling & Knowing: Making Minds Conscious](https://www.amazon.com/Feeling-Knowing-Making-Minds-Conscious/dp/1524747556/?tag=braipick-20)_** (_[public library](https://www.worldcat.org/title/feeling-and-knowing-making-minds-conscious/oclc/1284291484&referer=brief\_results)_), he makes the bold case that consciousness — that ultimate lens of being, which [shapes our entire experience of life](https://www.themarginalian.org/2017/05/25/christof-koch-consciousness-qualia/) and makes blue appear blue and gives poems their air of wonder — is not a mental activity confined to the brain but a complex embodied phenomenon governed by the nervous-system activity we call feeling.

Decades after Toni Morrison celebrated [the body as the supreme instrument of sanity and self-regard](https://www.themarginalian.org/2021/01/03/toni-morrison-beloved-heart/), neuroscience affirms the body as the instrument of feeling that makes the symphony of consciousness possible: feelings, which arise from the dialogue between the body and the nervous system, are not a byproduct of consciousness but made consciousness emerge. (Twenty years earlier — an epoch in the hitherto lifespan of neuroscience — the uncommonly penetrating Martha Nussbaum had anticipated this physiological reality through the lens of philosophy, writing in her superb inquiry into [the intelligence of emotions](https://www.themarginalian.org/2015/11/23/martha-nussbaum-upheavals-of-thought-neediness/) that “emotions are not just the fuel that powers the psychological mechanism of a reasoning creature, they are parts, highly complex and messy parts, of this creature’s reasoning itself.”)

[![Image 3](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/02/BeautifulBrain_p064.jpg?resize=680%2C887&ssl=1)](https://www.themarginalian.org/2017/02/23/beautiful-brain-santiago-ramon-y-cajal/)

One of neuroscience founding father Santiago Ramón y Cajal’s [little-known drawings of the brain](https://www.themarginalian.org/2017/02/23/beautiful-brain-santiago-ramon-y-cajal/).

Damasio’s premise rises from the flatland of earlier mind-based theories by a conceptual fulcrum both simple and profound:

> Feelings gave birth to consciousness and gifted it generously to the rest of the mind.

This view defies both extremes that dominate our present models of consciousness, each unimaginative and intellectually unambitious in its own way, as all extremes invariably are: materialism, which confines it to the neural activity of the brain, and mysticism, which places it entirely outside the contours of the body and beyond the reach of scientific investigation. Damasio writes:

> Any theory that bypasses the nervous system in order to account for the existence of minds and consciousness is destined to failure. The nervous system is the critical contributor to the realization of minds, consciousness, and the creative reasoning that they allow. But any theory that relies _exclusively_ on the nervous system to account for minds and consciousness is also bound to fail. Unfortunately, that is the case with most theories today. The hopeless attempts to explain consciousness exclusively in terms of nervous activity are partly responsible for the idea that consciousness is an inexplicable mystery. While it is true that consciousness, as we know it, only fully emerges in organisms endowed with nervous systems, it is also true that consciousness requires abundant interactions between the central part of those systems — the brain proper — and varied non-nervous parts of the body.

Drawing on the native poetics of our physiology, Damasio offers a definition of consciousness:

> Consciousness… is a particular state of mind resulting from a biological process toward which multiple mental events make a contribution… These contributions converge, in a regimented way, to produce something quite complex and yet perfectly natural: the encompassing mental experience of a living organism caught, moment after moment, in the act of apprehending the world within itself and, wonder of wonders, the world around itself.

[![Image 4](https://i2.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2016/04/darwinkidsdoodles1.jpg)](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/04/06/charles-darwin-children-doodles-origin-of-species/)

One of [the doodles Darwin’s kids left](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/04/06/charles-darwin-children-doodles-origin-of-species/) all over his manuscript of _On the Origin of Species_.

A century and a half after Darwin scribbled a note to himself in the margin of one of his manuscripts — “Never say higher or lower in referring to organisms… Say more complicated.” — Damasio details the levels of complexity by which various organisms manage the living wonder of themselves. All life-forms, from bacteria to Bach, share a basic machinery of stimulus-detection called _sensing_. Organisms with nervous systems are capable of _minding_ — the neurobiological process of mapping information into patterns and translating it into mental images.

These images furnish representations of the world, making it comprehensible and therefore survivable as the organism navigates that world by a sort of native biological intelligence that powers the basic self-care necessary for maintaining homeostasis — maintenance that eventually comes aglow with _feeling_. More complex organisms can manipulate those images, integrating them into a system of reference we call knowledge, which the nervous system makes explicit by creating patterns and committing them to memory, so that the organism can plan, reason, and reflect.

Ultimately, feeling conspires with minding and knowing to give rise to the system-level phenomenon of consciousness from the infrastructure of the nervous system and the body: Our perceptual senses — sight, touch, hearing, smell, taste — render the external world in mental images; our feelings render the internal world, representing in our own minds the state of our bodies — those roiling inner worlds in which all sense of wellbeing is won or lost. From this sense of ownership of ourselves arises the phenomenon of consciousness — the functions that makes possible the novel responses we call adaptation, or art.

Damasio writes:

> Consciousness gathers together the bits of sapience that reveal, by dint of their coincident presence, the mystery of belonging. They tell me — or you — sometimes in the subtle language of feeling, sometimes in ordinary images or even in words translated for the occasion, that yes, lo and behold, it is me — or you — thinking these things, seeing these sights, hearing these sounds, and feeling these feelings. The “me” and “you” are identified by mental components and body components.

[![Image 5](https://i2.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/bigwolflittlewolf8.jpg)](https://www.themarginalian.org/2017/10/12/big-wolf-little-wolf/)

Art by Olivier Tallec from [_Big Wolf & Little Wolf_](https://www.themarginalian.org/2017/10/12/big-wolf-little-wolf/) by Nadine Brun-Cosme

The most crucial of these bits of sapience manifest as mental images formed by body-mind interactions:

> Turn a mind inside out and spill its contents. What do you find? Images and more images, the sorts of images that complicated creatures, such as we are, manage to generate and combine in a forward-flowing stream. This is the very “stream” that immortalized William James and gave fame to the word “consciousness” because the two words were so often paired in the phrase “stream of consciousness.” But… the stream… is simply made of images whose near-seamless flow constitutes a mind.
> 
> 
> […]
> 
> 
> When we relate and combine images in our minds and transform them within our creative imaginations, we produce new images that signify ideas, concrete as well as abstract; we produce symbols; and we commit to memory a good part of all the imagetic produce. As we do so, we enlarge the archive from which we will draw plenty of future mental contents.

But it is the feeling coloring these mental images that makes our consciousness what it is — every perceived and stored scene or song, landscape or idea, is already infused with affect in the jar of memory, and that is what makes it shimmer with meaning.

Insisting that “we should celebrate the wealth and the messiness we have been gifted by affect,” Damasio writes:

> What you perceive or remember, what you try to figure out by reasoning, what you invent or wish to communicate, the actions you undertake, the things you learn and recall, the mental universe made up by objects, actions, and abstractions thereof, all of these different processes can generate affective responses as they unfold. We can think of affect as the universe of our ideas transmuted in feeling, and it is also helpful to think of feelings in music terms. Feelings perform the equivalent of a musical score that accompanies our thoughts and actions.
> 
> 
> […]
> 
> 
> Feelings are commingled with the things and events we feel thanks to the exceptional and intimate cross talk between body structures and nervous system.

[![Image 6](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/sougy_heart.jpg?resize=680%2C900&ssl=1)](https://www.themarginalian.org/2019/11/29/paul-sougy/)

_The Human Heart_. One of French artist Paul Sougy’s [mid-century scientific diagrams of life](https://www.themarginalian.org/2019/11/29/paul-sougy/). (Available [as a print](https://society6.com/product/paul-sougy-the-human-heart-1950s-proceeds-benefit-the-nature-conservancy_print?sku=s6-11999031p4a1v46?curator=brainpicker) and [as a face mask](https://society6.com/brainpicker/collection/vintage-science-face-masks?curator=brainpicker).)

Mapping the four-billion-year history of living organisms along its branching streams, Damasio envisions the distributary that led to us as a cascade of three evolutionary stages: _being_, _feeling_, and _knowing_, which continue to coexist in each of us modern sapiens, coursing through the various anatomical and functional systems that give us life. No invention of nature, Damasio argues, powered a greater leap than the emergence of nervous systems, which made minds possible — but their inception, like so many great inventions, was an unbidden byproduct of solving pressing necessities:

> Complex, multicellular organisms with differentiated systems — endocrine, respiratory, digestive, immune, reproductive — were saved by nervous systems, and organisms with nervous systems came to be saved by the things nervous systems invented — mental images, feelings, consciousness, creativity, cultures.
> 
> 
> Nervous systems are splendid “afterthoughts” of a non-minded, non-thinking, but pioneeringly prescient nature.

These astonishing afterthoughts of evolution became the stage on which the theater of consciousness plays out. Damasio explains:

> Nervous systems enable both complex movements and, eventually, the beginning of a real novelty: minds. Feelings are among the first examples of mind phenomena, and it is difficult to exaggerate their significance. Feelings allow creatures to represent in their respective minds the state of their own bodies preoccupied with regulating the internal organ functions required by the necessities of life… Feelings provide organisms with _experiences_ of their own life.

He considers how this transformative afterthought might have evolved and how it gave us the capacity for feeling that forever changed the course of life on Earth:

> Feeling probably began its evolutionary history as a timid conversation between the chemistry of life and the early version of a nervous system within one particular organism… Those timid beginnings provided each creature with an orientation, a subtle adviser as to what to do next or not to do or where to go. Something novel and extremely valuable had emerged in the history of life: _a mental counterpart to a physical organism_.
> 
> 
> […]
> 
> 
> Feelings… provide the urge and the incentive to behave according to the information they carry and do what is most appropriate for the current situation, be it running for cover or hugging the person you have missed.

[![Image 7](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/whatif14.jpg?resize=680%2C526&ssl=1)](https://www.themarginalian.org/2019/07/29/what-if-tallec-lenain/)

Art by Olivier Tallec from [_What If…?_](https://www.themarginalian.org/2019/07/29/what-if-tallec-lenain/) by Thierry Lenain

Through this essential feedback loop of feeling, we are able to assess how we are doing at the basic task of living — not only at the binary state of whether or not we are staying alive, but on the qualitative scale of how well our actual experience maps onto our optimal experience. Pleasure and pain, love and longing — these are all varieties of conscious experience that allow us to fine-tune our flourishing. They all arise when stimuli trigger molecular messages that travel from body tissues and organs, through nerve terminals, into the central nervous system and the brain, producing mental images that give us valuable information we experience as emotional states, which serve to steer us toward corrective action.

This might seem mechanistic and unpoetic, but out of this biological feedback loop arises our capacity for problem-solving and poetry, for beauty and transcendence, for everything we call creativity. In consonance with the consolation Lou Andreas-Salomé offered to her dispirited poet-friend Rainer Maria Rilke — [“A great deal of poetic work has arisen from various despairs.”](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/05/12/lou-andreas-salome-creative-block-rilke/) — Damasio observes:

> The human experience of pain and suffering has been responsible for extraordinary creativity, focused and obsessive, responsible for inventing all kinds of instruments capable of countering the negative feelings that initiated the creative cycle.
> 
> 
> […]
> 
> 
> Ultimately, we are puppets of both pain and pleasure, occasionally made free by our creativity.

This feedback loop of feeling is unavailable to organisms in the less developed _being_ stage of evolution, and yet out entire sense of being — the meta-awareness we experience as a _self_ — is contingent upon it. Damasio writes:

> Not surprisingly, feelings are important contributors to the creation of a “self,” a mental process animated by the state of the organism, and are anchored in its body frame (the frame constituted by muscular and skeletal structures), and oriented by the perspective provided by sensory channels such as vision and hearing.
> 
> 
> Once being and feeling are structured and operational, they are ready to support and extend the sapience that constitutes the third member of the trio: _knowing_.
> 
> 
> Feeling provides us with knowledge of life in the body and, without missing a beat, makes that knowledge conscious… The maps and images created on the basis of sensory information become the most abundant and diverse constituents of mind, side by side with ever present and related feelings. More often than not, they dominate the mental proceedings.
> 
> 
> […]
> 
> 
> Once experiences begin to be committed to memory, feeling and conscious organisms are capable of maintaining a more or less exhaustive history of their lives, a history of their interactions with others and of their interaction with the environment, in brief, a history of each individual life as lived inside each individual organism, nothing less than the armature of personhood.

[![Image 8](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/01/lieber3.jpg?resize=680%2C989&ssl=1)](https://www.themarginalian.org/2018/01/16/lilian-lieber-human-values/)

Illustration by Hugh Lieber from [_Human Values and Science, Art and Mathematics_](https://www.themarginalian.org/2018/01/16/lilian-lieber-human-values/) by Lillian Lieber

This understanding defeats a popular dictum of the self-help world — the comfort-blanket belief that one cannot cause another person’s feelings or be caused to feel a certain way by another person’s actions. No: One person can very much make choices and take actions toward another that impact and impair the other person’s homeostasis — that is, the organism’s sense of stability and safety — thus producing in that other person the negative feelings that are the organism’s feedback loop to protect homeostasis: pain, our primary signal for course-correction.

This is where our physiology and psychology converge. Offering neuoroscientific affirmation of Hannah Arendt’s searing philosophical-political indictment that [“society has discovered discrimination as the great social weapon by which one may kill men without any bloodshed,”](https://www.themarginalian.org/2017/01/30/hannah-arendt-jewishness-we-refugees/) Damasio writes:

> We are quite familiar with the direct way in which illness gives way to discomfort and pain or exuberant health produces pleasure. But we often overlook the fact that psychological and sociocultural situations also gain access to the machinery of homeostasis in such a way that they too result in pain or pleasure, malaise or well-being. In its unerring push for economy, nature did not bother to create new devices to handle the goodness or badness of our personal psychology or social condition. It makes do with the same mechanisms.

This is so because feelings are not purely mental phenomena but delicate interleavings of body and mind — the serpent of consciousness biting its own tail:

> The power of feelings comes from the fact that they are present in the _conscious mind_: technically speaking, we feel because the mind is conscious, and we are conscious because there are feelings… Feelings were and are the beginning of an adventure called consciousness.

[![Image 9](https://i1.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/04/creation_bhajjushyam2.jpg)](https://www.themarginalian.org/2015/04/15/creation-bhajju-shyam-gita-wolf-tara-books/)

Art by indigenous Gond artist Bhajju Shyam from [_Creation_](https://www.themarginalian.org/2015/04/15/creation-bhajju-shyam-gita-wolf-tara-books/) by Thierry Lenain

In the land of language, however, the adventure has been burdened by a great deal of cultural baggage, loaded with misconceptions and misuses. _Consciousness_ is a young English word, not yet born when Milton wrote that [“the mind is its own place, and in it self can make a Heav’n of Hell, a Hell of Heav’n.”](https://www.themarginalian.org/2014/02/13/william-blake-paradise-lost/) Today, particularly in [panpsychic theory](https://www.themarginalian.org/2021/08/17/annaka-harris-conscious/), it is often used interchangeably with _mind_, which plunders it of the essential role of feeling. Damasio points out that even in the older Romance languages, which include his native Portuguese, one must settle for the word _conscience_, already blunted by its multiple meanings. My native Bulgarian might come closest to Damasio’s model — the most literal translation of our word for consciousness is _self-knowledge_.

This, indeed, is the crux of Damasio’s case for feeling — feelings are how we know that our experience is our own, that the bodies through which experience courses are our own, that the perspective through which images flicker on the screen of the mind is our own. I am reminded here of something I once heard Gloria Steinem say, in the midst of a twenty-first century cultural dark age for conscience: [“The place where we need to go is where our bodies… are our own. This is the basis of democracy.”](https://pioneerworks.org/broadcast/gloria-steinem-ronan-farrow-vibe-theater)

With an eye to this essential parameter of ownership — the great revelation made possible by feeling — Damasio writes:

> Feelings let the mind know, automatically, without any questions being asked, that mind and body are together, each belonging to the other. The classic void that has separated physical bodies from mental phenomena is naturally bridged thanks to feelings… Self-reference is not an optional feature of feeling but a defining, indispensable one.
> 
> 
> […]
> 
> 
> What does it mean to say “I am conscious”? At the simplest level imaginable, it means to say that my mind, at the particular moment in which I describe myself as conscious, is in possession of knowledge that spontaneously identifies me as its proprietor… Some knowledge about the current operations of my body [and] some knowledge as retrieved from memory, about who I am at the moment and about who I have been, recently and in the long ago past… [produce] mental states imbued with feeling and a sense of personal reference.

At the heart of this idea is the loosening of the brain’s stronghold of consciousness and its diffusion through the entirety of the living organism — a reconfiguration that, as Damasio puts it, “requires the placement of that mind in the setting of its body.”

![Image 10](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2014/03/SFMoMA_brains.jpg?w=680&ssl=1)

Katharina Fritsch: _Display Stand with Brains_, 1989. (San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, 2009. Photograph: Maria Popova.)

This embodied model of consciousness looms with some profound consequences.

One, which Damasio does not address directly — perhaps because it is self-evident, or perhaps because he prefers not to ruffle the feelings (that is, the consciousnesses) of those who take flight from evidence in such beliefs — is a bold debunking of certain escapist fantasies from our creaturely reality: both the fantasies haunted by our parochial past and its various religious mythologies of an immortal soul that survives the death of the body (“soul” being the conceptual placeholder for consciousness before the word was coined), and the fantasies haunting the techno-utopian future with Silicon dreams of machine consciousness and technology-assisted ways of preserving human consciousness beyond the lifespan of the body by digitizing and migrating the contents of the brain alone.

Another, which Damasio does touch on at the end of the book, is a humbling antidote to the dual hubris with which humanity regards itself and other life-forms: the hubris of human exceptionalism across species, which presumes that our superior cognitive capacity relative to other animals automatically means superior consciousness (a hubris readily deconditioned by what we have been learning, for instance, about [the complex consciousness](https://www.themarginalian.org/2015/12/14/the-soul-of-an-octopus-sy-montgomery/) of the far more modest-brained octopus), and the within-species hubris that treats individuals with higher cognitive capacity measured by our [deeply flawed IQ metrics](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/11/30/siddhartha-mukherjee-the-gene-intelligence/) as superior to those with other, less computationally driven and computable forms of intelligence and sensitivity.

[![Image 11](https://i1.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/03/CephalopodAtlas16.jpg)](https://society6.com/product/art-by-friedrich-wilhelm-winter-from-cephalopod-atlas-by-carl-chun-1910-benefitting-greenpeace2663645_print?sku=s6-13477923p4a1v1?curator=brainpicker)

Art from [_Cephalopod Atlas_](https://www.themarginalian.org/2020/03/03/cephalopod-atlas-carl-chun/), the world’s first encyclopedia of deep-sea creatures. (Available as [a print](https://society6.com/product/art-by-friedrich-wilhelm-winter-from-cephalopod-atlas-by-carl-chun-1910-benefitting-greenpeace2663643_print?sku=s6-13477919p4a1v1?curator=brainpicker), a [face mask](https://society6.com/brainpicker/collection/vintage-science-face-masks?curator=brainpicker), and [stationery cards](https://society6.com/brainpicker/collection/vintage-science-face-masks), benefitting The Nature Conservancy.)

And this is the optimistic undertone I hear in Damasio’s model: By understanding as a full-body phenomenon the consciousness that lenses our view of reality and shapes our life-experience, we can not only become better stewards of our own bodies and of the planet we share with other bodies, human and nonhuman, but we can begin to dismantle the artificial hierarchies and categories by which we have long bolstered our creaturely centrality across the various scales and spectra of existence, from Ptolemism to anthropocentrism to racism, choosing instead to be both humbled and hallowed by the evolutionary wonder of consciousness.

In the remainder of **_[Feeling & Knowing](https://www.amazon.com/Feeling-Knowing-Making-Minds-Conscious/dp/1524747556/?tag=braipick-20)_**, Damasio goes on to detail the three universes of experience from which our mental images spring, how our chemistry and our skeletal frame converge to produce our sense of belonging to ourselves, the role of affect in how we allocate attention, and much more, including how the discoveries of science in the epochs since Emily Dickinson penciled her far-seeing verse have clarified her core insight:

> Dickinson was candidly committed to an organic view of mind and to a modern conception of the human spirit. And yet, in the end, what turned out to be wider than the sky was not the brain but life itself, the begetter of bodies, brains, minds, feelings, and consciousness. What is more impressive than the entire universe is life, as matter and process, life as inspirer of thinking and creation.

# The Art of Advancing with Age: Bertrand Russell on What Makes a Fulfilling Life

### By Maria Popova

[![Image 34: The Art of Advancing with Age: Bertrand Russell on What Makes a Fulfilling Life](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/07/portraitsfrommemory_russell.jpg?fit=320%2C520&ssl=1)](https://www.amazon.com/Portraits-Memory-Essays-Bertrand-Russell/dp/085124582X/?tag=braipick-20)

_“If you can fall in love again and again,”_ Henry Miller wrote as he [contemplated the measure of a life well lived](https://www.themarginalian.org/2014/06/26/henry-miller-on-turning-eighty/) on the precipice of turning eighty, _“if you can forgive as well as forget, if you can keep from growing sour, surly, bitter and cynical… you’ve got it half licked.”_

Seven years earlier, the great British philosopher, mathematician, historian, and Nobel laureate **Bertrand Russell** (May 18, 1872–February 2, 1970) considered the same abiding question at the same life-stage in a wonderful short essay titled **“How to Grow Old,”** penned in his eighty-first year and later published in [**_Portraits from Memory and Other Essays_**](https://www.amazon.com/Portraits-Memory-Essays-Bertrand-Russell/dp/085124582X/?tag=braipick-20) ([_public library_](http://www.worldcat.org/title/portraits-from-memory-and-other-essays/oclc/813603641&referer=brief_results)).

[![Image 35: bertrandrussell3](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2016/05/bertrandrussell3.jpg?resize=680%2C357&ssl=1)](https://www.amazon.com/Portraits-Memory-Essays-Bertrand-Russell/dp/085124582X/?tag=braipick-20)

Bertrand Russell

Russell places at the heart of a fulfilling life the dissolution of the personal ego into something larger. Drawing on [the longstanding allure of rivers as existential metaphors](https://www.themarginalian.org/2018/05/16/olivia-laing-to-the-river/), he writes:

> Make your interests gradually wider and more impersonal, until bit by bit the walls of the ego recede, and your life becomes increasingly merged in the universal life. An individual human existence should be like a river — small at first, narrowly contained within its banks, and rushing passionately past rocks and over waterfalls. Gradually the river grows wider, the banks recede, the waters flow more quietly, and in the end, without any visible break, they become merged in the sea, and painlessly lose their individual being.

In a sentiment which philosopher and comedian Emily Levine would echo in her [stirring reflection on facing her own death with equanimity](https://www.themarginalian.org/2018/05/24/emily-levine-ted-reality/), Russell builds on the legacy of Darwin and Freud, who [jointly established death as an organizing principle of modern life](https://www.themarginalian.org/2017/07/10/adam-phillips-darwins-worms-life-death/), and concludes:

> The man who, in old age, can see his life in this way, will not suffer from the fear of death, since the things he cares for will continue. And if, with the decay of vitality, weariness increases, the thought of rest will not be unwelcome. I should wish to die while still at work, knowing that others will carry on what I can no longer do and content in the thought that what was possible has been done.

[**_Portraits from Memory and Other Essays_**](https://www.amazon.com/Portraits-Memory-Essays-Bertrand-Russell/dp/085124582X/?tag=braipick-20) is an uncommonly potent packet of wisdom in its totality. Complement this particular fragment with Nobel laureate André Gide on [how happiness increases with age](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/01/28/andre-gide-aging-happiness-death/), Ursula K. Le Guin on [aging and what beauty really means](https://www.themarginalian.org/2014/10/21/ursula-le-guin-dogs-cats-dancers-beauty/), and Grace Paley on [the art of growing older](https://www.themarginalian.org/2015/09/03/grace-paley-aging/) — the loveliest thing I’ve ever read on the subject — then revisit Russell on [critical thinking](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/05/18/bertrand-russell-free-thought-propaganda-doubt/), [power-knowledge vs. love-knowledge](https://www.themarginalian.org/2017/05/08/bertrand-russell-the-scientific-outlook/), [what “the good life” really means](https://www.themarginalian.org/2015/02/03/bertrand-russell-immortality-good-life/), [why “fruitful monotony” is essential for happiness](https://www.themarginalian.org/2015/01/21/bertrand-russell-boredom-conquest-of-happiness/), and his [remarkable response to a fascist’s provocation](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/10/06/bertrand-russell-oswald-mosley/).

# Love in the Time of Dinosaurs

### By Maria Popova

In 1824, studying a set of large fossil bones discovered in a quarry near Oxford two centuries earlier, the English theologian, geologist, and paleontologist William Buckland kept looking at the fragment of the lower jaw. Something didn’t add up. As he examined it more closely, he realized these were not the remains of an elephant, as previously thought, but of an enormous carnivorous reptile with no analogue in the fossil record or in the living world.

He christened it _Megalosaurus_ — the first named dinosaur — and set out to compose a complete account of the ancient beast.

Because nobody knew what dinosaurs looked like, he needed an exceptional scientific illustrator whose unbridled imagination and disciplined draughtsmanship could enflesh the bones of the mysterious creature. Taken by a particularly excellent drawing of the jaw of an extinct hyena, he obtained a letter of introduction to the artist, tucked it into his coat pocket, and boarded a coach across Devonshire, hoping to be received.

William took one book to accompany him on the long ride — a weighty new volume by paleontology founding father Georges Couvier, summarizing his pioneering research on the fossil bones of quadrupeds. With gaping disbelief, he watched another passenger take out that same book and begin paging through it. The conversation was inevitable and the realization quick: She was the artist he was traveling to meet. Cuvier himself had sent her the book in gratitude for her contribution.

![Image 36](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/marymorland_hyena.jpg?resize=680%2C529&ssl=1)

Mary Morland’s watercolor of hyaena jaw, 1822. (The Royal Society)

Perhaps because she had lost her mother while still an infant, Mary Morland had grown up fascinated by deep time, by the slow-burning beauty of minerals, by the way fossils immortalized the ephemerality of the flesh. After devouring Couvier’s books as a teenager, she taught herself draughtsmanship and unlearned what her culture had told her she could be: Determined to become an artist of science, she sent her specimen illustrations to Couvier himself.

The venerable scientist was so taken with the young woman’s work that he published it alongside his studies. Word spread across the scientific community and soon she was illustrating other books and modeling rare specimens in leather.

![Image 37](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/marymorland.jpeg?resize=680%2C398&ssl=1)

Miniature of Mary Morland circa 1840. (Oxford University Museum of Natural History)

Unlike most women of her time, whose standard path to subsistence was marriage, Mary could now make a living by her own work. If she married, it would only be for love. Her love was the science of time: She kept drawing paleontological specimens, grew an impressive mineral collection, became a fossil geologist herself.

By the time she met William that day on the coach, she was an old maid in her late twenties and one of the era’s most esteemed scientific illustrators. They started on the dinosaur work immediately.

![Image 38](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/MaryBuckland_Megasaurus_Marginalian.jpg?resize=680%2C426&ssl=1)

Lithograph of Megalosaurus jaw specimen after Mary Morland, 1824. (Oxford University Museum of Natural History)

Within a year, Mary Morland was Mary Buckland. Their home became a miniature Alexandria of science books, light pouring in from candle-holders made of ichthyosaurus vertebrae, fossils lining every sideboard. Their dining room housed a menagerie of frogs and snakes. Guinea pigs ran regularly across the table. A pony occasionally rode past, a laughing child on its back.

One of their surviving children would later recount that Mary not only illustrated William’s studies but, with her “great mental powers, habits of perseverance and order, tempered by excellent judgment,” she “gave to them a polish which added not a little to their merit.”

![Image 39](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/bucklands_TheMarginalian.jpg?resize=680%2C554&ssl=1)

Silhouettes of the Bucklands collaborating as their young son plays with a fossil under the worktable. (_The Life and Correspondence of William Buckland_, 1894)

Despite their fourteen-year age difference, she outlived him by just over a year, channeling her bereavement in studying marine bryozoans — coral-like saltwater creatures — with her daughter. Hours before her death, Mary was still bent over her microscope, entranced by a new specimen.

Mary and William were buried alongside one another, their entwined fossils to be discovered by some paleontologist of the far future: What is love if not the mutual belonging of our passions and our bones.
